strengths: Addresses a genuine and practical problem in multi-task manipulation: static camera viewpoints causing occlusion-induced perception failures, illustrated convincingly in the motivating example (Fig. 1).

The combination of an active viewpoint exploration policy (MVEP) with a task-aware Mixture-of-Experts visual encoder (TaskMoE) is a reasonably novel architectural contribution, and the decoupled gating (NG < NJ gates) is a sensible mechanism for balancing parameter sharing and specialization across heterogeneous tasks.
The proposed pseudo-environment interaction mechanism to avoid costly online RL rollouts is a practical engineering contribution that could be useful beyond this specific application.

Evaluation spans 18 RLBench tasks plus a small real-world robot deployment (5 tasks), together with ablations, sensitivity studies on view count/camera radius, and a zero-shot generalization test for TaskMoE, giving a reasonably broad (if not deep) empirical picture.

Per-task analysis shows large gains on occlusion-prone tasks (e.g., insert peg +17.6 points, put in cupboard +6.4 points, slide block +7.2 points), which supports the core hypothesis that dynamic viewpoints help when occlusion is a dominant failure mode.
weaknesses: The headline average improvement (86.7% vs. 84.9% for ARP+) is modest and not uniform: several tasks regress substantially under TAVP (e.g., stack cups drops from 80.0% to 60.0%, place cups drops from 48.8% to 44.0%, screw bulb drops from 89.6% to 88.0%), which weakens the claim of "domain-wide gains rather than isolated spikes."

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for RLBench evaluations, which are known to be noisy (typically single evaluation runs with 25-100 episodes); given the small absolute margins in many tasks, statistical significance of the claimed improvements is unclear.

The "w/o Active Exploration" ablation (random viewpoints) causes a catastrophic collapse to 8.89% success, which seems implausibly extreme and is not well explained; this raises questions about whether the fine-grounding/rendering pipeline is simply poorly conditioned for arbitrary views rather than cleanly isolating the value of the learned exploration policy.

The sensitivity analysis (Table 3) and TaskMoE generalization analysis (Table 5) use a different, much smaller training regime (20 demos/task, 5-6 tasks) than the main results (100 demos/task, 18 tasks), making it hard to reconcile these numbers with the main results or generalize conclusions from them.
Real-world results are purely qualitative (Fig. 4, Fig. 7) with no quantitative success-rate table for the 5 real-world tasks, limiting the strength of real-world validation claims.
Zero-shot generalization is tested on a single OOD task ("open drawer") with a low absolute success rate (12%), which is too narrow a basis to strongly support broader generalization claims.

No comparison against other 3D-aware or viewpoint-adaptive baselines mentioned in the related work (e.g., 3D Diffuser Actor, SAM2Act), limiting the assessment of TAVP's advantage relative to the current state of the art beyond RVT2/ARP/ARP+.

Component-level cost/ablation analysis is incomplete: the three reward terms (task loss, entropy, diversity) in MVEP are not individually ablated, and parameter/compute overhead of TaskMoE vs. MVEP is not broken down.
Minor presentation issue: an apparent stray watermark/text ("Zhouxia") appears in Figures 1 and 3, which could be an artifact of incomplete anonymization or figure preparation.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: fixed camera viewpoints in multi-task manipulation cause occlusion and incomplete scene understanding, and the paper proposes a principled solution combining active view (re-)rendering with task-conditioned feature routing.

The method is evaluated broadly: 18 RLBench tasks with multiple strong baselines (RVT2, ARP/ARP+, 3D Diffuser Actor, Act3D, PerAct, etc.), plus real-world experiments on 5 tasks, ablations, sensitivity analysis on view count/radius, zero-shot generalization, data-efficiency, and inference-latency comparisons -- a commendably thorough evaluation protocol for a systems-style paper.

The pseudo-environment / shadow-network mechanism for optimizing the viewpoint policy via PPO without costly physical rollouts is a practical and reasonably well-motivated engineering solution to a real training bottleneck.

The TaskMoE design (instruction+scene-conditioned routing via cross-attention/FiLM, decoupled gates vs. experts) is a sensible extension over naive task-ID routing and is shown to help both known and (to a lesser extent) unseen tasks.
Real-world deployment and robustness testing under occlusion, illumination change, and unseen objects/backgrounds provide some evidence of practical applicability beyond simulation.
weaknesses: Ablation results are internally inconsistent and under-explained: removing active exploration and using purely random viewpoints collapses performance from 86.7% to 8.89%, while removing TaskMoE only drops performance by ~1.1pp on the same 18-task benchmark (Table 2), yet a separate 5-task ablation (Table 6) shows TaskMoE nearly doubling success rate (24.0% -> 49.6%). These contradictory magnitudes across tables are not reconciled or discussed, undermining confidence in the reported component contributions.

The overall gain over the strongest fixed-view baseline (ARP+: 84.9%) is modest (86.6%), and per-task results show TAVP underperforms baselines on several tasks (e.g., Put in Safe, Stack Cups, Place Cups), so the claim of 'domain-wide gains' is only partially supported by the per-task table.

Real-world evaluation is limited in breadth (5 tasks, 10 trials each) and only compared against a single baseline (Diffusion Policy), which is architecturally very different from TAVP's fixed-view RVT2/ARP-style competitors used in simulation; a real-world comparison to RVT2/ARP+ would be more informative and is notably absent.

The zero-shot generalization claim rests on a single unseen task (Open Drawer) with a low absolute success rate (12%), which is a weak empirical basis for the strong generalization claims made in the text.

The 'dynamic camera' framing is somewhat misleading: viewpoints are not physically acquired but rendered from an aggregated point cloud reconstructed from the fixed cameras; this reliance on accurate global point-cloud reconstruction (acknowledged as a limitation for reflective/transparent objects) means the method's benefits may be overstated relative to genuinely acquiring new physical observations, and the practical applicability in scenes with substantial reconstruction/depth noise is unclear.

Several tables (3, 6, 7) lack variance/error bars, and few evaluation episodes (e.g., 10 real-world trials per configuration) leave the statistical reliability of many claimed improvements (especially smaller ones) unclear.

Presentation issues: the reference list contains unedited placeholder entries (Frobnicate, entries [1]-[6]), which is a sign of insufficient proofreading and template cleanup, though this alone is not a technical weakness.

The three-stage training pipeline (fixed-view pretraining, PPO-based MVEP fine-tuning, joint fine-tuning) adds meaningful complexity and hyperparameters (reward weighting, radial constraints, gate/expert counts) whose sensitivity is only partially explored, raising reproducibility concerns for practitioners without the exact codebase/settings.
